questions.objective: I.G.2 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Mixing
questions.text: Before using a micropigmentation pigment, the technician should

answers.text: add distilled water to all pigments to standardize consistency
heat the pigment bottle in hot water for 5 minutes to activate the color
shake or roll the pigment bottle gently to redistribute settled particles before dispensing
pour a small amount into a separate sterile pigment cap for single-client use

explanations.d: Dispensing into a single-client pigment cap is correct practice for infection control, but it is done after the bottle has been properly shaken or rolled to homogenize the pigment — not as a substitute for this preparation step.
explanations.a: Adding water to pigment without manufacturer guidance alters the pigment concentration, preservative ratio, viscosity, and pH, potentially compromising color accuracy and product stability; only manufacturer-specified diluents should be used when dilution is indicated.
explanations.b: Heating pigment bottles in hot water can degrade heat-sensitive organic pigment molecules, denature preservatives, and accelerate the breakdown of stabilizing components; it is not a standard pigment preparation step.
explanations.c: Micropigmentation pigments are suspensions in which solid pigment particles are dispersed in a liquid carrier; over time, the denser pigment particles settle toward the bottom of the bottle by gravity; gently shaking or rolling the bottle before use redistributes the pigment particles evenly throughout the carrier, restoring the correct particle-to-carrier ratio and ensuring consistent color concentration and viscosity in the dispensed pigment.

questions.name: Scientific Concepts
questions.objective: I.G.2 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Mixing
questions.text: When mixing two pigment colors to create a custom shade, the technician should

answers.text: document the exact brand, color names, and volumetric ratios used so the formula can be reproduced at future appointments
mix directly in the original pigment bottle to preserve sterility of both pigments
use only colors from different manufacturers to avoid chemical incompatibility
mix colors in a reusable glass dish that is disinfected between clients

explanations.a: Custom color mixing is a common technique in micropigmentation to achieve precise shade matching for individual clients; detailed documentation of the mixing formula — including the specific brand and color name of each pigment used, the exact volumetric or drop-count ratio, and any diluent added — is essential for reproducing the same custom shade at touch-up or enhancement appointments; without this documentation, color matching relies on visual memory and guesswork, often producing visible inconsistency.
explanations.b: Mixing directly in the original bottle contaminates the entire supply with the second pigment; if the formula does not work as intended, the entire bottle is now altered and unusable in its original form; custom mixing must always occur in a separate single-use pigment cap.
explanations.c: Using pigments from different manufacturers is common in custom color mixing; the standard concern is not cross-manufacturer incompatibility but rather that pigments within a manufacturer's line are formulated to be compatible — some cross-brand mixing may introduce unknown interactions, but this is assessed on a case-by-case basis rather than avoided universally.
explanations.d: A reusable glass dish that is disinfected between clients presents cross-contamination risk because chemical disinfection of porous or scratched surfaces may not achieve the sterility required for items that contact the pigment to be implanted into a client's skin; single-use pigment caps are the standard container for procedure-day pigment dispensing and mixing.

questions.objective: I.G.2 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Mixing
questions.text: Adding a white pigment containing titanium dioxide to a colored pigment will

answers.text: deepen and intensify the original color by adding opacity
make the mixture more transparent and suitable for shading techniques
produce a more opaque, lighter tint of the original color that heals cooler and can appear grayish in darker skin tones over time
neutralize the color entirely, producing a neutral beige regardless of the original hue

explanations.a: Titanium dioxide is a white pigment, not a color-deepening agent; adding a white to a color creates a lighter, more opaque tint — the opposite of deepening or intensifying the original hue.
explanations.b: White pigments containing titanium dioxide increase opacity rather than transparency; adding titanium dioxide reduces the ability of the mixture to create a soft, transparent shading effect.
explanations.c: Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) is an inorganic white pigment with high refractive index and opacity; mixing it with a colored pigment creates a lighter, more opaque tint of the original color; in lighter skin tones this can produce desirable pastel or softer shades; however, titanium dioxide tends to heal with cooler (pinker or grayer) undertones than originally applied, and in medium to darker skin tones the white titanium content can create an ashy or grayish appearance over time as the warm melanin in the overlying skin optically modifies the cooler white-tinted pigment visible beneath — an important color theory consideration in shade formulation.
explanations.d: White pigments do not neutralize hue in the color theory sense of complementary cancellation; neutralization (hue cancellation) requires mixing complementary colors (e.g., red + green); adding white to a color produces a tint, not a neutral.

questions.objective: I.G.2 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Mixing
questions.text: Mixing organic and inorganic pigments in a single formula requires caution because

answers.text: organic pigments are always darker than inorganic pigments, creating unpredictable lightening when combined
inorganic pigments require refrigeration while organic pigments require room temperature storage, creating incompatible storage conditions
they use different carrier solutions that are chemically incompatible in all formulations

organic and inorganic pigments can have different rates of fading, chemical stability, and long-term color shift — organic components may fade faster while inorganic components (especially iron oxides and titanium dioxide) remain, changing the apparent color of the mixture over time

explanations.a: The relative darkness of organic vs. inorganic pigments depends on the specific pigments mixed; there is no universal rule that organic pigments are always darker; the key concern is differential fading and color shift over time, not initial color depth.
explanations.b: Standard micropigmentation pigments — both organic and inorganic — are stored at similar room temperature conditions; incompatible storage requirements are not the primary concern when mixing the two types.
explanations.c: Many commercial micropigmentation pigments already combine organic and inorganic colorants in the same carrier system; cross-carrier chemical incompatibility is not a universal rule for all organic-inorganic combinations.
explanations.d: Organic pigments (azo dyes, carbon black) and inorganic pigments (iron oxides, titanium dioxide, ultramarine) have fundamentally different photostability and chemical stability profiles; organic molecules are more susceptible to UV-induced photodegradation and can fade relatively faster than the physically stable mineral particles of inorganic pigments; in a mixed formula, as the organic component fades selectively, the remaining inorganic component dominates the visible color — producing an unwanted color shift that differs significantly from the original result; this long-term color drift is a critical formulation consideration when combining organic and inorganic pigment types.

questions.objective: I.G.3 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Rehydration
questions.text: A micropigmentation pigment that has thickened or partially dried in the bottle should be rehydrated using

answers.text: distilled water added directly to the bottle
the manufacturer-specified diluent or rehydration solution at the recommended amount
rubbing alcohol to thin the consistency
saline eyedrops available at any pharmacy

explanations.a: Adding distilled water directly to a pigment bottle without manufacturer guidance alters the carrier solution chemistry, preservative concentration, pH, and viscosity in ways not tested by the manufacturer; this can compromise pigment stability, sterility, and color performance.
explanations.b: Manufacturers formulate specific diluents or rehydration solutions that match the pH, ionic composition, and preservative profile of their pigment formulas; using the manufacturer-specified product for rehydration restores the original pigment characteristics without altering the formula's tested safety and performance parameters; adding any other liquid — even seemingly neutral water — changes the product outside its tested specifications.
explanations.c: Rubbing alcohol (isopropyl or ethyl alcohol) is a solvent-antiseptic, not a pigment diluent; adding alcohol to a pigment formula can denature preservatives, alter pigment particle suspension stability, change pH dramatically, and produce a formula that is unsafe to implant into the skin.
explanations.d: Pharmacy saline eyedrops contain preservatives (such as benzalkonium chloride), tonicity agents, and pH buffers formulated for ocular use — not for micropigmentation pigment rehydration; these additives can interact unpredictably with pigment chemistry and are not tested or approved as pigment diluents.

questions.objective: I.G.3 — Knowledge of Storage and Care of Pigment: Rehydration
questions.text: Pigment that has become thick and difficult to work with during a procedure should

answers.text: be diluted with the client's own blood to maintain biocompatibility
be heated over a flame to reduce viscosity before continuing
be discarded and replaced with fresh pigment from a new single-use cap dispensed from a properly stored bottle
be thinned by adding a drop of the topical anesthetic in use during the procedure

explanations.a: Using the client's own blood as a pigment diluent introduces bloodborne pathogen-contaminated material into the pigment cap; this contaminates all remaining pigment, creates a biohazardous liquid that cannot be properly controlled, and risks splattering or mishandling of blood — this practice is unsafe and violates fundamental infection control standards.
explanations.b: Heating pigment over an open flame introduces fire risk in the studio, could overheat and chemically alter the pigment components, and creates an uncontrolled temperature change that could injure the technician or client; flame heating of cosmetic products is never an appropriate practice.
explanations.c: Discarding thickened mid-procedure pigment and switching to a new single-use cap from a properly stored bottle is the correct response; thickening during a procedure may indicate that evaporation of the carrier solution has concentrated the pigment, that the pigment was not properly mixed before use, or that the cap has been exposed to excessive air; fresh pigment from a properly prepared cap ensures consistent viscosity and color performance for the remainder of the procedure.
explanations.d: Topical anesthetics are formulated for surface analgesic application; they contain active anesthetic agents, preservatives, vasoconstrictors, and pH buffers not intended as pigment diluents; mixing anesthetic into pigment creates a chemically undefined compound that has not been tested for implantation and could cause unexpected tissue reactions.
